articles.title: The Xbox Wireless Controller X25 Special Edition Is Now Available, Get it for Possibly $10 Less With Coupon
articles.summary: Inspired by the look and feel of the original OG Green Xbox console.
articles.body:
The X25 Special Edition Xbox wireless controller was officially unveiled in June during the Xbox Games Showcase and preorders are finally shipping out. If you haven't yet pulled the trigger on this one, there may be an additional incentive to do so. Walmart , among other retailers, has it in stock for $79.99 with free delivery. However, there's a $10 off coupon code " SAVE3X " that appears to works on this controller. Your mileage may vary (it might not work for you) but we've confirmed that it is working for some people. Here are the coupon code's official terms and conditions from Walmart:

Valid on your first three online pickup or delivery orders

Only for new customers (although it actually works for many returning customers)

New Release: X25 Special Edition Xbox Wireless Controller

Xbox Wireless Controller X25 Special Edition

Also available at other retailers for $79.99

The official Microsoft Xbox controller is considered by many to be the best Xbox and PC controller under $100 . The X25 Edition is a special release that celebrates Xbox's 25 year anniversary. It features a translucent green shell that is reminescent of the OG green Xbox that was released way back in 2003. Outside of the color scheme, this is the tried and true Xbox controller we are accustomed to. Standard features include textured grips, hybrid D-pad, button mapping with the Xbox app, a 3.5mm audio jack that works with any wired headset, and a Share button to upload screenshots and video. The controller is cross platform and will work on both Xbox and PC. For PC, you can either connect a USB Type-C and use it as a typical wired controller or you can connect wirelessly over Bluetooth.

Eric Song is the IGN commerce manager in charge of finding the best gaming and tech deals every day. When Eric isn't hunting for deals for other people at work, he's hunting for deals for himself during his free time.

articles.title: Zach Cregger's Resident Evil Movie Outpacing Alien: Romulus, Backrooms, and Obsession at the Global Box Office
articles.summary: It might have been controversial at first for daring to adapt the feel of the games rather than the story and characters, but Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil is a massive success. The horror flick has passed $360 million at the global box office, and is outpacing some big horror hitters.
articles.body:
It might have been controversial at first for daring to adapt the feel of the games rather than the story and characters, but Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil is a massive success. The horror flick has passed $360 million at the global box office, and is outpacing some big horror hitters.

After last weekend's $22.6 million haul, Resident Evil is now on $361.1 million worldwide, a figure that makes it the highest-grossing Resident Evil movie ever, and Cregger's biggest commercial hit. According to box office watchers , at the five weekend mark, Resident Evil is outpacing Alien: Romulus ($330 million), Backrooms ($331 million), and Obsession ($287 million).

Resident Evil could hit $400 million by the end of its run, putting it ahead of Sinners ($370.4 million), but it may struggle to overtake Backrooms and Obsession's final figures ($400.6 million and $522.8 million respectively). Both those movies had remarkable staying power in theaters, fueled by strong word of mouth. Indeed, Obsession is the fifth highest-grossing horror movie of all time (unadjusted for inflation).

Resident Evil has done particularly well in China, where $56 million has been made so far. The Resident Evil movie has proven so popular that it helped boost sales of the Resident Evil 2 remake on PS5 by 50% . It also inspired The Walking Dead star Chandler Riggs to publish a fan film take on Resident Evil 7, in a bid to work with Cregger on a sequel.

But will Cregger actually get the chance to make a follow-up, or does he even want to? In September, Cregger says he’d love to tell more stories in the Resident Evil universe, admitting he already had "ideas" about where he'd take things in Resident Evil 2 .

Cregger’s take on Resident Evil is currently the highest rated video game movie adaptation of all time with critics, beating Sonic the Hedgehog 3. IGN’s 8/10 Resident Evil movie review called it “a simple and exciting survival horror story that benefits greatly from Zach Cregger’s sensibilities.”

The Super Mario Bros. movie remains the highest grossing game adaptation of all time , followed closely by its sequel and A Minecraft Movie. Of course, these family friendly movies will always have more of a chance to succeed than a movie where corpses fall from windows and splat onto a snowy street.

Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. Find him on Twitter @MckKirk

articles.title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Is an Fun Collection of Sports Minigames Designed to Spark Deceptively Heated Rivalries - Review
articles.summary: A collection of sports games designed to spark deceptively heated rivalries.
articles.body:
Back in 2022, Nintendo attempted to revive the fun and charm of the motion-controlled Wii Sports era, but it didn’t quite live up to that lofty goal. Now in 2026, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort takes another swing at that same difficult feat with a clear focus on “more.” More sports, more outfits, more modes, and more collectibles. That doesn't always translate to a better package, with Sports Resort often feeling a wide ocean rather than a deep diving pool, but it more than makes up for it with a broad range of games ripe to bust out at the next big party. So while it may not clear the high bar set by the original Wii Sports in 2006, it still brings out the same child-like joy.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is a collection of 12 different sports minigames, ranging from highly competitive one-on-one Table Tennis to leisurely cruising in a prop plane around Wuhu Island where they all take place. The quality of each game varies drastically. Archery is a standout thanks to its unique use of the Joy-Con controllers, while a returning sport like Basketball is largely untouched and still feels too choreographed – it's once again missing the freedom of movement and control I want so desperately from a potential party version.

The new sports can also be hit and miss. Power Cruising uses two Joy-Con held like you are gipping handlebars to simulate racing a jet ski, but those clunky controls don’t always work well, so it feels more like a gimmick rather than a fun sport. On the other hand (quite literally),Thumb Wrestling helps bring whimsy to the package. It’s extremely silly, but actually makes for some competitive matches – in my online sessions, I was pleasantly surprised with how strategy and tactics changed from match to match. Watching players develop new ways to trick and bait their opponents into getting caught in their trap was entertaining, and I found myself determined to never let anyone get the best of me.

Archery is easily the best sport offered in Sports Resort. With four different courses scattered around Wuhu Island, it feels the most well-thought out. I stretched out my arms in front of me, holding both Joy-Con perpendicular to the floor, then clicked the ZL button with my left hand and drew it back to my chest like I would draw a real bow. Using my right Joy-Con to aim at a distant target, it was satisfying every time I hit my mark. More challenging courses and hidden targets to find help flesh out Archery overall, which meant it provided hours of fun for my friends and I in a way many of the thinner options don’t.

As you might expect, playing through Sports Resort by myself proved to be a bit lackluster, as it lacks the competitive spirit so intrinsic to the games it recreates. Island Crown, a new mode that has you climb the ranks in nine of the 12 sports, pushed me forward with a little bit of structure and challenge, but even then I found my enthusiasm waning before too long.

Its loose story has you defeat challengers in order to eventually face the island champion, who – depending on the sport – will either taunt or cheer you on after every victory. Upon defeating one of the island champions you'll unlock a few more extra objectives in the given sport. Sometimes it's an Island Legend looking for a fight, others it’s a gauntlet of challengers that need to be defeated without losing. It's a decent distraction for those looking to casually play sports while your friends and family aren't around to party, and that’s about it.

But when they are around, Sports Resort is easily the game I want to break out. So much of the joy of these games is heightened when folks in the room are cheering, yelling, and getting so into it you need to remind everyone to keep the Joy-Con wrist strap on. This has always been the spirit of the Nintendo Sports games, and Sports Resort is one of the best versions of it around when you've got the crew to play.

Recruiting my roommates to run through the sports on a Sunday afternoon was an eye-opening experience. Games like Volleyball – which I found to be incredibly boring during my time with Island Crown and casual single-player – became electric back and forth rallies that lit up the room. Exhausted cheers, disappointing sighs, and questionable calls made even some of the more mundane sports like Golf feel exhilarating.And quick, snappy menus make hopping between sports seamless as well, which kept everyone from zoning out between rounds.

Even leisure sports like Skateboarding quickly became heated competitions as we slammed our Joy-Con on the table in mouse mode, ready to race. Skateboarding is the only game in Sports Resort that takes advantage of this control scheme, effectively turning the Joy-Con into a mini Tech Deck. Intuitive controls like flicking your hand to the left or right did 360 pop shuv-its and quickly lifting the front it off the table produced an ollie. With multiple race courses, we ripped through each one attempting to best one another, constantly pushing for faster times as our rivalry grew.

My only real complaint about the local multiplayer is that games like Boxing and Power Cruising require participants to have two Joy-Con each, meaning you aren't able to play those sports at all if you only have the single pair that came with the Switch 2. So if you're planning on having folks over to box or ride Jet Skis, ask them to bring some extra controllers.

When we needed to cool down, we hopped into the Sightseeing Tour mode, which allows you to zoom around Wuhu Island in search of points of interest marked with giant floating cameras. Collecting a camera marks it on your Sightseeing Log and gives you a little flavor about that part of the island. It's a neat way to get a sense of how all of the sports fit together contextually in this space, and allows you to visit other islanders while they compete on the tennis courts, archery ranges, and more.

Between Archery rounds or Thumb Wrestling matches, I would routinely hop into my Prop Plane to fly around the island in search of more Sightseeing Logs. The five-minute timer makes it an excellent bit sized adventure that rewards you for exploring a different part of the island on each outing. Going off the beaten path proved fruitful every time, with plenty of secrets to find for those willing to be curious.

It would be really easy for Sports Resort to be nothing more than a series of menus as you bounce between sports, with no connective throughline to follow. Sightseeing Tour gives everything a sense of place, and strengthens the quirkiness found on the outskirts of it all. Blimps fly high in the sky, speedboats race into the distance, and plenty of characters can be found hanging in parts of the island you would never see by just playing the basic sports. Leisure sports also offer a free roam mode which allows you to explore to your hearts content.

That said, sports like Tennis, Basketball, Thumb Wrestling, and a few others have just one set location each, which does get old. I wish there was more variety in where they could be played across Wuhu Island, because it became unexciting to see the same background for my 30th Thumb Wrestling match – even if the Mii's in the background were different from the match before.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Screenshots

If your friends are farther away, Sports Resort has online play with both casual and pro-league options. Casual uses a lobby system that allows multiple people to party up and play games together. If a two-player game is selected, you can even form multiple huddles in the same lobby, playing separate sports at the same time. However, there is no way to spectate someone else's game, which is a bit of a let down. I would love to be able to watch friends play Tennis or take out their aggression in a Thumb Wrestling match.

Each sport also has special modes that change up the gameplay just enough to be fresh for a bit, but I didn't find any of them exciting enough to return to time and time again. Bowling adds its classic obstacles to the lane, which require more creative strategies and fancy footwork to overcome, while Archery has four people compete for points on the same target, attempting to avoid an opponent's section as you hit your own. These modes are a fun break, but don't go much further beyond that.

Everything you do in Sports Resort also nets your Spocco Points, which can be spent at a rotating shop. The shop sells themed items in a set, and 1,000 Spocco will get you one item randomly pulled from that set. You won't receive duplicates, but it is strange that you can't just choose the items you want. Being forced into a random roll feels like it just artificially inflates the amount of Spocco needed to get what you want.

The customization is rather robust at least, with no shortage of fancy outfits, namecard titles, face paints, and so much more – you’ll unlock bevy of different options by playing Island Crown as well, ranging from leather studded gloves for Thumb Wrestling to unique volleyball attire. I was constantly gaining Spocco, and while it was a little tiresome to be frequently reminded to check out the shop as I earned points for miscellaneous things like shaking the Joy-Con 1,000 times, at least the rewards for doing so were neat.

articles.title: Final Fantasy Resonance Video Review - IGN
articles.summary: Final Fantasy Resonance reviewed by Michael Higham on Nintendo Switch 2."Part of playing through Final Fantasy Resonance is to examine why an older era of RPG was wedged into our psyche for so long. The rose-tinted glasses can be strong at times, but so too was the sharpness of their messages, and the ones we remember most fondly understood that simple did not mean shallow. And that's the biggest thing Resonance couldn't really nail down. Even with weaker dialogue that fills large stretches of its story, the journey is still worth embarking on. Resonance is special for how it wields HD-2D as an art style to set a new, higher standard that goes well beyond nostalgia. It's the flair that makes a solid turn-based combat system more satisfying when beating down a staggered boss. And it's what paints its world as an exciting place to explore, especially when a superb soundtrack backs up each moment before hitting you with a nasty battle theme. Although I'm left underwhelmed by pieces of the storytelling itself, I'm glad Final Fantasy Resonance exists to revive Brave Exvius but also show that old-school style RPGs can keep raising the bar in more ways than one."

articles.title: Antigravity just halved the price of its drone — by swapping its headset for wristwatch control
articles.summary: What it’s like to try the $800 Antigravity A1 Follow Me set, with watch and ring controllers instead of an FPV headset.
articles.body: Last year’s Antigravity A1 is the best beginner drone I’ve ever tried. I put a friend who’d never flown into its virtual cockpit and didn’t worry one bit. The A1’s also nice for people who’d prefer to think about flying rather than filming, because you can reframe its 360-degree footage after. [Media: But until today, that meant wearing the company’s FPV goggles and spending upwards of $1,599 on the complete set. Now, Antigravity is halving the price of entry to $799 in the US with a new “Follow Me” kit that replaces the original headset and motion controller with a wristwatch and ring instead. The idea is that Antigravity can be your robot cameraman, automatically flying, following, and filming you with a minimum of gear. I took the new kit for several test drives this fall, and I’m cautiously impressed. Instead of powering on a headset and finding a safe place to sit while you block out the world, you can now pull a drone and a watch out of your bag, power them both on, hold a button to launch the drone from your hand, then walk or ride while the Antigravity A1 automatically films and follows you, dodging obstacles along the way. You can even wave your arm like a magic wand to nudge the drone left, right, down, up, towards, or away while it’s filming. You get a swipeable preview of what the drone sees on the watch’s touchscreen, and can select various quickshots there or summon a couple of sliders (forward/backward, ascend/descend) to manually fly the A1 out of a jam. The ring doesn’t do anything you can’t already do with the watch; it’s just an extra button so you can launch and reposition it one-handed. [Image: The ring is just a button, and technically the watch is a modular screen you could attach to other mounts too — there’s a quick release button to detach it from the watchband frame. As I discovered after three crashes, the A1 is not yet intelligent enough to dodge everything or stay with me through thick and thin. I took it all around my neighborhood on a kick scooter, and you might want to be careful around power lines, thin branches, or the vertical guy wires holding utility poles in place. There’s also a lot of rough edges I hope Antigravity will fix, like the sluggish experience swiping around the touchscreen, or how it won’t land on my hand without switching back to manual mode, or how I can’t get it to automatically start tracking and filming me — I always have to find myself on the watch screen, tap on myself, then tap another button to begin. I also ran into an issue where it wouldn’t follow me once I crested a high hill, because it thought it was flying at too high an altitude. Most of all, I hope Antigravity will figure out how to keep the drone from drifting out into the street or over a neighbor’s fence when I tell it to follow right behind. It’s far smaller than me, so anywhere I go, I feel like it should fit! But as you’ll hopefully see in my video higher up this story (also on Instagram/TikTok) it’s not bad at following me through a dense suburban environment! None of my crashes so far have crippled the drone, and I like how the watch automatically plays the last seconds of footage from before a crash. It made it very easy to find the drone after. [Image: Antigravity’s price chart is so comprehensive, I decided to share it in its entirety. Antigravity’s new full-coverage propeller guards can also help in case of impact; I saw the drone bounce right off one obstacle and keep flying. They’re included in the $799 set, though existing Antigravity A1 owners can buy the accessories too: it’s $340 for the watch and ring, and $40 for the guards, with a 20 percent discount for those who can prove they already own the aircraft. Antigravity’s A1 is kind of like the folding Skydio I wish that company had made before it left consumers behind to serve industry instead. The self-flying Skydio 2 similarly had a few crashes in my tests and wouldn’t always stay in its lane. But I’ve long wanted a folding version I could easily stick in a bag, and the Antigravity A1 seems like the next best thing. [Image: You can remove the propeller guards fairly easily; there’s room in the kit’s bag for all four of them plus the folded drone, whose cameras are now protected by a new quick-release cover.

articles.title: Final Fantasy Resonance Sets a Higher Bar for HD-2D and Brings the RPG Series Back to Turn-Based
articles.summary: Final Fantasy Resonance retools Brave Exvius and sets a new benchmark for HD-2D visuals alongside solid turn-based combat and incredible music, which carry an underwhelming story.
articles.body:
To evoke the classics is also to hold yourself to the high standard set by them. With Final Fantasy Resonance bringing the venerated series back to its origins with turn-based combat, and wielding Square’s HD-2D art style to modernize nostalgia for the pixel art era, it plucks at something I've longed for as someone who grew up in the SNES generation. While I've expressed my love for the Octopath Traveler series time and again, Final Fantasy has of course crystalized into something meaningful over the past several decades. But as much as Resonance looks like a torchbearer for classic RPGs, it also goes for a style of storytelling that often rings hollow. So, I think of it as a game of moments – when a genre-fusing boss theme graces your ears, when you execute a turn perfectly and watch all your spells fire off with big damage numbers, and when a cutscene brings HD-2D to life in a way you've just never seen before.

Resonance adapts the story and characters from the now-shuttered mobile game Final Fantasy: Brave Exvius by packaging them into the structure of a traditional RPG; no gacha mechanics, no microtransactions. It's quite similar to what Square Enix did with Octopath Traveler 0 and it's a brilliant way to bring existing stories into a format I'm a lot more inclined to play. With that comes an overworld with towns to represent each region, random encounters, an airship for roaming free and discovering pieces of land that feel like secrets, and full voice acting throughout the main story.

It largely sticks to the events of the first season of Brave Exvius, which follows the knights from the Kingdom of Grandshelt, Rain and Laswell, the mysterious magical girl born from a crystal, Fina, along with additional friends on a quest to stop the armor-clad Sworn Six from destroying the world's crystals and plunging it into calamity. Of course, there's more beneath the surface. That said, a lot of dialogue and interstitial events have been added to fill out the journey, which took me about 45 hours to complete (including all of the side quests marked on my map and poking around the overworld for optional minibosses who offer intense challenges). While chunks of Resonance's story aren't very riveting, the production value here had me forgetting that this was built on the bones of a mobile game – not that Brave Exvius was any lesser of an achievement for what it was.

That retooling extends to gameplay, which retains concepts and mechanics that work extremely well as an engaging turn-based combat system – and hearing "turn-based" and Final Fantasy in the same breath after all these years released those good chemicals in my brain, too. This is not an ATB system with an active element, but a straightforward turn order along a timeline. And the way you either plan accordingly depending on which units are up or manipulate the order to your advantage had me employing similar strategies as I do in the Trails series or the Octopath Traveler games.

It's all about elemental affinities and staggering enemies in Resonance, however. Each party member has their own set of elements covered through magic spells or element-imbued physical attacks, but they also equip what are called Visions that function somewhat like a Job system directly inspired by Final Fantasy V. This is what provides flexibility in party composition, giving you the tools to make sure you either cover all the elements or go all-in on a specific type so you can streamroll bosses. While every attack chips at an enemy's stagger meter, hitting their weaknesses is, of course, the strategy demanded of you.

I'm of two minds with this system: while it’s nice to have flexibility as you swap Visions between party members to constantly change their overall movesets, it can sometimes trivialize your combat approach. For example, going into a water-themed boss fight, I knew purely electric builds were going to be the optimal strategy. So, while it was rad as hell to watch chunks of stagger and HP get chopped off as I spammed electric attacks, I often didn't feel the need to think much harder than that. Having the foresight to anticipate the right element before a fight isn't quite as rewarding as being pushed to scheme with what you have.

Compare this to the boost and break system of an Octopath Traveler, where the tools you're given are more dynamic and free-flowing even with elemental affinities involved, which then lets you get more creative rather than just having you hammer away with one specific element. I cruised through the first half of Resonance since most enemies and bosses were pushovers. But thankfully, things got tougher in the late game where they hit harder and inflicted more status ailments to work around. Key moments where I was challenged to think steps ahead culminated in some real hard-fought battles toward the end.

Overall, it still provides enough of the puzzle-esque tactical thinking that's required of a good turn-based RPG. Party members level up alongside their mastery of equipped Visions, but you have to manually rank up Visions then apply passive perks and support spells, which gets into some interesting buildcrafting that gives a little extra depth that mattered for those big fights. And I enjoyed Resonance's combat system because it still captures the satisfaction of teeing off on a staggered enemy with your nastiest spells, especially because their animations look so good and hit with emphatic impact.

Michael Higham's Personal Final Fantasy Rankings

Visions themselves are super fun to toy with because most of them are avatars of star characters from Final Fantasy's past. Their movesets call back to specific spells and signature attacks from their respective games, and it's nice to see parts of the series' history celebrated in a way that's integral to how Resonance plays. Staggering an enemy grants extra turns in a bonus phase, and staggering all of them (or a lone foe) leads to the sweeping stagger phase where everyone gets to pile on, which then concludes in a Resonance attack tied to a Vision of your choosing. I still find it jarring to go from beautiful HD-2D to a CGI cutscene (pulled from Brave Exvius) when summoning a Resonance attack, some of these are pretty cool, like big Shanttoto throwing a massive boulder of dark energy or Clive getting ready to hit L3+R3 to accept the truth. There's some wonderful pixel art around those cuts that look incredible, too, like Lightning, who gets a full animation set here – and it's lovely to see these characters recreated in that style.

Each is obtained by visiting shrines sprinkled throughout the overworld and going through a quiz-like dialogue sequence that walks through the events of their own stories (and beware, there are some major spoilers for Final Fantasies you have not played yet). I found this pretty cheesy at first, but it really grew on me as a reminder of how each entry captured something powerful that has stood the test of time. You never really know which shrine belongs to who, so when their music kicks in, it had me grinning ear-to-ear – and as someone who was deeply touched by FFXIV Shadowbringers, hearing "Tomorrow and Tomorrow" and recounting Y'shtola's ongoing story is a prime example of how sometimes Resonance got me.

More than the hard-fought battles against god-like beings, Final Fantasy has stuck around and won our hearts because of the stories it tells. And this is where I wrestled most with Resonance. The foundations of its story are quite solid and consistent as a classic Final Fantasy about the power of crystals that fuel these magical worlds and defeating evil to save the world against villains who reveal themselves to be more complicated by story's end. But it's always about how those stories get told and the impactful themes they explore along the way. Resonance has glimpses of hitting those same highs, yet I found long stretches of its storytelling to be quite underwhelming.

Taking the story of Brave Exvius and expanding on it was definitely worth exploring, but Resonance fills out a lot of that time with dialogue that feels like it was written for a middling young adult novel then crammed into a fantasy world. Not that fantasy stories need to be Shakespearean or high-concept, but much of Resonance reads like a script that didn't get punched up; overly talkative where it takes five lines for something that could've been said in one, and banking on a contemporary twee tone and some mustache-twirly villains. I love melodrama, long cutscenes, and tropes like the power of friendship, and Resonance has that for sure, but doesn't start dialing it in until late in the game.

But there's still something enticing about going on a journey with characters who overcome unbelievable odds. I came around on lead protagonist Rain and his brother-in-arms Lasswell because, while simple characters, they have a bond that riled me up for the conclusion. Fina turns out to be a little bit more than someone with a mysterious, dark past and was a compelling way to weave in more of the magical storytelling devices sensibly. The stern tactician Nichol and pink-haired mage Sakura turn out to be the better written characters who fit the RPG mold so well; and the emotional arc Nichol goes through is genuine and one of the few ways the story shows some depth. However, I struggled to care about the Sworn Six since a lot of their dialogue undersells their importance to the broader lore. And that Dr. Lazarov is an incredibly annoying throwaway who is nothing more than a mad scientist to roll your eyes at.

Resonance also struggles with narrative momentum because it's shrouded in a vagueness that blurs its throughline rather than luring you in. So, it relies more on the societal issues of each region – environmental tragedies, revolt against a tyrannical government, or underclasses being exploited. These stories are delivered decently on their own, but the thematic coherence didn't come until much later, and how it all tied together through the mysterious ways of magic was predictable, if not fine.

Now, it usually takes more than spectacle to win me over, but Final Fantasy Resonance is an exception. When it matters most, the strongest moments are uplifted with some of the best cutscene work in HD-2D, wielding camera movement in a 3D plane effectively as character sprites and pixelized special effects coalescence through fluid animation that conveys emotion dialogue wouldn't be able to capture alone. The art style may have been born out of nostalgia, but Resonance proves that we're past that point and it can lead to new, evocative ways of creating worlds and elevating stories beyond the sum of their parts.

Music also plays a large role in why I look back at my time with Resonance fondly. It may be the expectation for a Final Fantasy game to have an amazing soundtrack, but the way certain town themes employ instruments that instill the feeling of a brutal, industrialized empire or a mystical city floating in the sky is magical. From the normal battle theme to the different tiers of bosses, I realized that Brave Exvius' great soundtrack was here all along and played off of many of the musical themes attached to the series. Remixing a dungeon theme into a bouncy electronic tune was like having fire come out of my headphones. And my jaw dropped when I heard a boss theme remix that had piano jazz fused with orchestral metal, a double bass drum pedal, and a latin choir that in a way that came together in unexpected harmony; it's such an impressive song I still can't get out of my head. Sometimes music resonates more powerfully than words, and it's one of the things I'll remember most.

articles.title: Final Fantasy dips back into the SNES golden era with Resonance
articles.summary: Final Fantasy Resonance is Square Enix’s latest HD-2D game, blending gorgeous pixel art and detailed 3D graphics with retro turn-based battles and a familiar style of story.
articles.body: Final Fantasy is a lot different than it used to be. While many of the early Final Fantasy titles look and play similarly to each other, the series has since grown to encompass blockbuster games like Final Fantasy XVI and the gargantuan Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, which don’t play much like the classics. But there’s still an audience for retro RPGs and old-school Final Fantasy games, especially thanks to the HD-2D style that mixes gorgeous pixel art with detailed 3D graphics to great effect. Square Enix has made a bunch of HD-2D games already, like the remakes of early Dragon Quest titles, but this week, it’s launching the first HD-2D Final Fantasy game: Final Fantasy Resonance. Resonance, thanks to the HD-2D art, kind of looks like what the classic Final Fantasy games feel like in my memory, but I was surprised at how old-school Resonance feels to actually play, too — which, for the most part, is a good thing. In Resonance, I’ve spent a lot of time wandering around a big world map to get from place to place, tackling random battles along the way and investigating little sparkles to pick up items. The towns have a familiar feel, with the classic inn, item shop, and weapons shop setup. Similarly, battles are traditional turn-based fights, so I’ve found myself spending a lot of time in various battle menus to plan out my attacks. Enemies even flash right before they attack, just like in older RPGs. [Image: At times, Resonance can almost feel rudimentary; I’ve recently been working my way through Final Fantasy VII Remake again ahead of Revelation, and Remake’s action-heavy fights feel much more contemporary. But there’s something soothing about Resonance’s familiar patterns. I really like just grinding through some random baddies to level up. The story is pretty standard fare, at least during the 10 hours I’ve played. You play as Rain, a plucky blonde hero who is morally pure and fights for those less fortunate than him. After a great magical crystal is destroyed, you and your best bud Lasswell head out on an adventure to stop the destruction of other crystals. So far, Resonance’s story hasn’t done a lot to innovate on a familiar formula — I’ve already come across two people who have amnesia, a JRPG staple — but it all moves along breezily enough that it’s not a huge deal. Resonance isn’t all old-school, though, as there are a lot of modern touches. In fights, enemies have health bars and stagger bars, forcing you to be strategic instead of just mashing basic attacks; it’s usually smarter to whittle down a stagger bar by exploiting weaknesses through magic and skills. You can speed up fights and even skip long attack animations (of which there are many). On the world map, you can fast travel to any location you’ve already visited, which is especially useful during the multipart side quests. In dungeons, you can teleport from a save near a boss fight back to the entrance if you need to resupply before a big battle. [Image: Resonance also lets you bring in characters from other Final Fantasy games to aid you in battle. (It’s a holdover from Resonance’s roots as a mobile title; the game is an “adaptation” of the first story arc of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, which was shut down in 2024.) As you move through Resonance, you’ll recruit “Visions” of characters like Final Fantasy VI’s Terra Branford or Final Fantasy VII’s Cloud Strife, and each of the game’s characters can “equip” one Vision to give them new moves in battle. Over time, while using a Vision with a Resonance character, you unlock more moves and abilities that you can use even when you don’t have that Vision equipped. It’s a clever system that offers a lot of possibilities for interesting builds, making the hunt for more Visions feel like more than just a way to get a hit of nostalgia. But I’m already getting sucked into Resonance like I used to with classic Final Fantasy titles. At one point, as I was nodding my head to heart-pumping music during an intense boss fight on a moving train, I realized I was completely absorbed by the game in a way that only a Final Fantasy can pull off. The game’s old-school structure with modern improvements lets Square Enix have it both ways, as the old-school approach sits comfortably alongside a big-budget game like Final Fantasy XVI. The series has come a long way since the games that Resonance uses as inspiration, but it pulls in enough from newer titles that playing it feels like enjoying the best of both worlds. Final Fantasy Resonance launches on October 22nd on Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X / S.

articles.title: The Truth About Bigfoot Is Revealed in the Fascinating Documentary Capturing Bigfoot, New to Prime Video
articles.summary: New to Prime Video: Capturing Bigfoot is an essential documentary not just about the infamous mythical creature, but the human beings who exist in the long shadow that it casts too.
articles.body:
Capturing Bigfoot is playing in select theaters and is available to rent or buy on Prime Video starting October 20.

Bigfoot is alive and was born in Yakima, Washington.

Keep your hairy suits on; the mythical creature is not alive alive in the same way you and I are. However, he remains alive in the public imagination. One of the primary reasons for this, as seen in director Marq Evans’ fascinating documentary Capturing Bigfoot, has to do with a short film made way back in 1967 by a group of Washingtonians that supposedly captured footage of the creature walking with a memorably lumbering gait in the remote woods of California. The infamous Patterson-Gimlin film, named for two of its creators, Roger Patterson (who died in 1972) and Robert “Bob” Gimlin, has continued to endure over the decades, picked apart by doubters just as it is still held up as almost a sacred document by believers.

It’s a subject that’s ripe for deeper analysis, and Capturing Bigfoot – which premiered back at this year’s SXSW Film & TV Festival, where it already began to make waves in the Bigfoot community – not only delivers on that front, but also in its look at the people who made the 1967 film. It’s a solidly entertaining watch, bringing to light the reality of what's out there lurking in the woods, but it also offers something more in how it gets at the deeper, more painful, and yet still beautiful psychological mysteries living inside the human mind.

While Evans gives plenty of attention to the Bigfoot of it all and the hold it has over so many, critically, he’s not making a film that’s solely about the creature. Instead, that is, if anything, merely the entry point to something far more illuminating. With patient, incisive filmmaking and thoughtful care, Evans uncovers not only the truth about the Patterson-Gimlin film – and the being it “captured” – but also infinitely more valuable revelations about the people who made it and those who now have to live with its legacy. While this all builds to a genuinely stunning revelation by showing what is essentially the most significant “deleted scene” in Bigfoot cinema history, it's the journey of getting there that makes Capturing Bigfoot a consistently compelling gem. You come to see all of not only who Roger Patterson was, but the impact his film had on his son, Clint, as he sorts through his father’s legacy. Is Roger a trickster who lied to his son and everyone he knew? Is he a filmmaker in his own right who made an enduring work of cinema? Or is he just another struggling hustler who was trying to carve out his piece of the ever-elusive American dream?

Ultimately, the Patterson patriarch was trying to tell a story that, yes, he could use to make some money, but it became much more than that. To both those who knew him and many who didn’t, his film became something that provided so much over the years. We hear this not just from Clint, but also those like the late Bigfoot expert (and academic) Jeffrey Meldrum, who attended a screening of the film as a child shortly after it was made. The experience left an impact on Meldrum and gave him something to believe in as an adult, so to then hear it may have all been premised on a lie is a psychologically difficult thing to reckon with. As Meldrum says at one point, sounding more than a little anxious, he feels like he’s being led “up to a precipice and you’re just about to push me over the edge.” When he later watches new footage that upends everything that he’d come to believe about Bigfoot, we see in his eyes that so much of his worldview and life’s purpose is crumbling.

Even as this could all seem rather silly or, even worse, cruel or exploitative, Evans never looks down on his subjects or seeks to take advantage of them. There is a compassion to the filmmaking, even as the subjects are made to confront the lies that surround them and have shaped their lives. Evans asks the tough questions when he needs to and doesn’t shy away from the more thorny reality of what actually happened, but he also works to understand what it was about the film and Bigfoot that still means so much to many of those he talks to.

Whether the Patterson-Gimlin film is a fake or not, it’s not going to stop people from believing in Bigfoot or anything else that they need to. It’s not about what makes factual sense, but what makes emotional sense and allows such folks to feel like they have some agency over the stories in their lives. There is a painfully tragic dimension to this, as such ideas are inherently built upon buying into a delusion, but it’s also a deeply human, occasionally darkly humorous, and potentially dangerous reality of our world. Even as Capturing Bigfoot doesn’t fully dive into the more expansive implications of this, it does reveal the darker truths and lies that can exist within all of us. There will always be the things we build our lives around and hold closely to. This one just happened to take the form of a giant, hairy cryptid. Thus, while the physical being may not be real, there will always be more Bigfoots. Bigfoot is dead. Long live Bigfoot.

articles.title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos and Top Features
articles.summary: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort has arrived to provide gamers with peak nostalgia.
articles.body:
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort has arrived to provide gamers with peak nostalgia.

It's been 20 years since the iconic Wii Sports captured people's attention and transformed the gaming landscape. It will always be difficult to compete with the memories people have of their time playing Wii Sports but Nintendo has managed to hit the mark once again.

Now with the advanced hardware of the Switch 2 and its Joy-Cons, people can experience the non-stop excitement and tension better than ever. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is perfect for all ages and sure to be a staple for years to come at game nights, especially at gatherings this holiday season.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort features 12 competitions and Nintendo did a great job featuring a nearly-entire lineup of unique sports to avoid overlapping skillsets and becoming repetitive. Although Tennis and Table Tennis may seem similar at a glance, they play differently enough due to the style of play that it's understandable to include both, especially since the motion controls are so responsive and smooth for swinging to hit the ball.

The other 10 competitions are extremely varied, featuring Archery, Basketball, Bowling, Boxing, Golf, Thumb Wrestling and Volleyball, plus three sports that fall in the 'Leisure' category, Prop Plane, Power Cruising, Skateboarding.

Archery returns from Wii Sports Resort and feels far more enhanced given the improvement in technology. Using both Joy-Cons to emulate holding a bow and arrow, pulling back one Joy-Con to 'extend a bow' while aiming with the other Joy-Con before finally releasing a shot feels surprisingly smooth and effortless. Archery demands precision, concentration and adapting to both distance and wind physics depending on the map. There's definitely a learning curve, especially when it comes to recognizing the proper distance and wind speed while aiming, but there may not be a better feeling in the entire package than nailing a bullseye. It's easy to see Archery becoming one of the most intense competitions among friends and family during parties, especially as rivals try to distract each other.

For Basketball, players can choose different competitions such as a three-point content or a shooting streak, in addition to a two vs. two game. As expected, this is one of the most active competitions in the game. It's a lot of rapidly moving the Joy-Con up and down in order to dribble towards the basket or get in position to try to steal a pass. Players can swipe for a steal as well but positioning is extremely important, especially since shooting the ball is rather forgiving and will make players feel like they're Golden State Warriors superstar Stephen Curry at times. It certainly makes for a fun time and the shooting competitions will really help players get comfortable with the mechanics and should be a staple at parties.

Golf is another iconic game from the original Wii Sports and essential to include here. As expected, gamers can select from three different courses of varying difficulty. The motion controls are impressively accurate, recognizing even a slight twist in the wrist when swinging. Of course, there's obstacles to take into consideration like trees, plus weather, to make for a life-like experience. Golf has been a mainstay here for two decades because it translates perfectly to motion controls and the form factor, plus advanced technology of the Joy-Cons, makes it the best way to play yet.

Bowling is better than ever thanks to the new Joy-Cons. The one-to-one motion of bowling is extremely intuitive, allowing players to adjust for speed and the spin of the ball to get rotation. Often a staple at parties, it wouldn't surprise if it reigns supreme from this package because it run flawlessly. It's an impressive display of perfect motion controls and the best version of one of the most successful games in franchise history.

There may not be a better display of the success of Nintendo Switch Sports Resort than Boxing. The motion controls are flawless, reacting to each punch and movement from the player. While holding the Joy-Cons upright, players can block their face and body from incoming punches, dodge from left to right and accurately swing to the opponent's face or body. With a game like this where motion controls, timing and input lag will make or break the experience, it was immediately reassuring just how perfect everything came together. As soon as any movement happens, it is happening on the screen without any delay as if the player was standing in the ring inside the screen. Boxing can easily become one of the staples at parties because it is active, intense and exciting (but make sure to use the safety straps with the Joy-Cons to avoid them flying out of hands).

In Tennis, players can choose to play doubles with up to four people or a laid-back match with two people featuring a slow-moving ball. Players can choose to play on a hard court, clay court or grass court, which naturally cause games to play differently like in real life. The difference in surface is certainly noticeable so it makes for one of the more varied competitions in the package. When playing solo, the players by the net do a great job not interfering or hogging returns so it feels more like a one vs. one match, which is a wise design choice to avoid taking the player out of the experience. Overall, tennis is as enjoyable as ever. It's a staple for a reason because it's among the most accessible and entertaining games featured.

Table Tennis is far different from Tennis, requiring a different type of skill set to be featured. Here, it's much more about managing the corners of the table, the spin of the ball and the slice. It requires deliberate placement of the ball during the volley and finally setting up a power shot to catch the opponent off guard. The motion controls and timing is flawless here, which is crucial because any type of delay or lag could really ruin the experience since Table Tennis requires such precision.

While Thumb Wrestling may be an unconventional choice, Nintendo deserves credit for its inclusion because it is extremely accessible. While technically all of the competitions could be played sitting down, Thumb Wrestling is by far the most accessible and the mechanics simply work . It likely won't be a staple for many but does offer its own tension, quirkiness and charm. It may be an easy one to overlook compared to others but it definitely serves its purpose in a tournament setting and especially to include with younger or older players.

Volleyball may be the game that requires the most practice because it can be difficult to nail down the timing of and navigate the screen due to the camera perspective. The control scheme to bump, set, spike and block is intuitive and the motion is impressively instantaneous, which is why some people may have difficulty timing exactly when to make an action, resulting in being too early or late. It's great that the CPU partner if playing solo or with an odd number of people is helpful in playing their role and it shouldn't feel like somebody is playing from a disadvantage in those scenarios.

For the three 'Leisure Sport' options, Prop Plane is first up and allows players can go on a sightseeing tour of the island or fly freely. Sightseeing Tour is far more fun than it sounds as players will have five minutes to collect photos throughout the massive island and can shoot a blaster to pop balloons while listening to some smooth, catchy jazz music. It's similar to a mashup of Star Fox action and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater collecting, so it's definitely a mode worth checking out. A third mode is strictly multiplayer with 2-4 people and is a battle mode where players will compete to capture the most balls against each other within two minutes. Players can unlock different maps/courses for this. Utilizing a single Joy-Con to control the plane's movement by simply tilting up, down, left or right, Prop Plane is one of the most accessible modes perfect for younger players, elderly or casual gamers. It's a great way to introduce somebody to familiarize them with the Joy-Con's motion controls.

Power Cruising is another 'Leisure Sport' and like Prop Plane, it includes the same type of Sightseeing Tour and free roam. For Wave Race fans, the third mode is Sea Sprint race riding through rings for speed bursts, with various courses available to choose from. Players hold out their arms horizontally while pressing the ZL and ZR buttons to move forward. Even though this is considered a 'Leisure Sport,' players will likely wish they were going faster as some may grow tired holding out their arms for the nearly two minutes it takes to complete the course.

The final 'Leisure Sport' is Skateboarding, once again consisting of the type of modes as Prop Plane and Power Cruising. This may feel like the most 'tech demo' of sorts for people because it requires holding the Joy-Con like a mouse and moving it backwards to mimic somebody gaining speed pushing their foot off the guard. The impressive tech of the Joy-Cons allows players to use even their thigh or any surface to perform this act and it's magically excellent.

Throughout the countless hours players can spend playing Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, gamers will earn rewards for achievements and milestones, which will allow players to unlock many wardrobe items to customize their character. There's a weekly and monthly rotation of items to keep players active and coming back to obtain everything. There's even certain themes for what's offered, which won't be spoiled since it'll be a fun surprise when entering the shop. It's a nice touch to give players something to strive for beyond getting the best of their friends, family or random opponents online. Of course there's a tutorial about how to play each sport but there's also advice on how to strategize and succeed, which is surely to be helpful for many gamers as they familiarize themselves with the motion controls.

Like Nintendo Switch Sports on the original Nintendo Switch in 2022, gamers can play against other people online. It's truly the complete package for players looking for this style of game.

Overall, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is another successful outing for Nintendo. For the past 20 years, Nintendo has impressively bridged the gap for all ages to come together and enjoy different competitions featuring motion controls.

Although there will always be people wanting more competitions to be included, especially since we've experienced some of these staples many times like Tennis and Bowling, it would be a real shame if these weren't included given how much fun they are. For the sports that are included, Nintendo has mastered the gameplay, making them all feel comfortable to play as if somebody was playing the real sport. Now on Nintendo's most advanced hardware to date, the motion controls feel smooth, responsive and effortless.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort releases at the perfect time ahead of the holiday season. From reminiscing about the glory days of Wii Sports to creating new memories (and rivalries), this is a fantastic choice for any party. Given how accessible it is and the endless multiplayer fun to be had, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is a worthy contender for these categories at The Game Awards.

articles.title: Final Fantasy Resonance Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos and Top Features
articles.summary: Final Fantasy Resonance from developers Square Enix and Lancarse is a first for the fabled series.
articles.body:
Final Fantasy Resonance from developers Square Enix and Lancarse is a first for the fabled series.

Resonance is the first Final Fantasy game to roll out the HD-2D format while adapting a portion of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, originally a mobile game from 2015.

Adapting a mobile game with gacha elements will elicit a no-thanks from some, but there was a heartfelt memorable story there. That Square Enix wants to surgically remove that and give it an almost Octopath Traveler-style treatment is pretty telling.

Granted, it's brutally difficult to stand out in a golden era for the RPG scene right now. Resonance will need to resonate (sorry) quite a bit to live up to the hype its series namesake usually generates.

Stunning would be the right word for Resonance.

There have been other recent HD-2D attempts in gaming. But this feels like the first to really nail it, with the character sprites really looking like they belong in the world and popping off the screen.

The surrounding, varied detail is a treat and holds attention, of course. The fine detail and even draw distances in the background of fights are impressive. So, as always, are the particle effects and other goodies in battle. It's just an overall sense of heart pumped into this one that really creates some immersion.

Credit goes to another fantastic Final Fantasy soundtrack and overall sound design, too. That includes the fully-voiced cutscenes to crank up the production quality to top-tier levels.

The twist on traditional RPG turn-based combat, if one could even call it that, is the presence of a timeline at the top of the screen. It's a fun way to see the exact order of a battle in digestible format, permitting deeper-than-expected strategizing.

It's not just seeing and prepping for a big enemy attack, either. The stagger system is one way this is quite a bit more engaging than it probably should be. Planning around enemies' attacks or other types of moves by plotting how and when to fully deplete a foe's stagger gauge (elemental weaknesses play a role) removes their turn and quickly becomes a key to battle.

That stagger system plays into the game's namesake, too. Players can weave "Visions" into their combat as summons and triggering a stagger of the entire enemy team at once will trigger a "Resonance" super attack alongside one of the visions.

There are real summons, too, called espers. Once called into battle, they assist players for three turns before executing a finishing move. As expected, it's a huge investment to get these summons on the field, but totally worth it.

It's all just different-feeling enough to stand out on its own and, short of just being simply fun, it's a cool idea to see some iconic cast members of the series return to help out via those visions.

The story here is as Final Fantasy as it gets. Rain, the protagonist, commands an airship squadron alongside his best friend tasked with investigating a shrine that houses a magical barrier. A crystal within the shrine gets shattered by a baddie and off things go.

Players romping through the world to defend crystals from an evil army while mysteries unravel and rosterable companions pop up isn't anything new in the RPG sphere. It's just all about execution.

And it's great. The pacing feels good and this isn't just nostalgia fodder via those visions. The cast is easy to care about and memorable, even if the background foundation of the story is pretty standard.

There are lots of little small things to find out in the world. It's not just completionist fodder, either, as exploration will turn up new Visions to use in combat, esper summons, and other notables. As a locale, the setting is a character in its own right.

Hitting on the same themes again, overall progression hits the expected stuff with some small interesting twists. Leveling up and managing the inventory is one thing. But the scale of how things change by simply equipping different visions to each party member is pretty wild. It's the same story for summons, too. Kitting out a party for a specific elemental weakness of a boss looks quite a bit different on a per-player basis and the overall strategizing that goes into party construction is deep.

Resonance arrives with a long list of options in the menus, from difficulty customization to the always-appreciated ability to tweak the battle speed to get things moving faster.

The eyes can gloss over a bit at all the RPG remakes and reimaginings and sheer quantity of the genre coming out these days.

There are tried and true staples of Final Fantasy here when it comes to story, characters, worlds and combat. But the small layerings atop especially the battle formula really make it stand out. So much so, in fact, it's worth wondering if the mainline series, never mind competitors, don't take inspiration from just how good this all feels together.

It's all enough to make Resonance a splendid time and, frankly, one of the better RPG releases in a stacked 2026 lineup.

articles.title: Former Call of Duty Dev Says 'It's Hard to Watch' Xbox Make Money From Black Ops PlayStation Ports
articles.summary: A former Call of Duty designer has argued that developers should get royalties when older games are ported to new systems, saying it's "hard to watch" Xbox make money from the recently released and hugely successful Black Ops 1 and 2 ports on PlayStation.
articles.body:
A former Call of Duty designer has argued that developers should get royalties when older games are ported to new systems, saying it's "hard to watch" Xbox make money from the recently released and hugely successful Black Ops 1 and 2 ports on PlayStation.

Former Treyarch level designer Gavin Goslin took to LinkedIn to discuss the PS5 and PS4 re-releases, which he said amounted to Microsoft and Activision "printing money off of work completed over a decade ago."

The pair of games reportedly sold 11.2 million copies combined in July, earning around $435 million in one month, according to estimates from Alinea Analytics (thanks, VGC ). “The recent Black Ops 1 and Black Ops 2 digital drops on PlayStation proved a couple of things,” Goslin said. “First, today’s gaming landscape is starved for the tight, high-quality experiences we used to get. Second, these legacy titles are still massive money-makers for Activision and Microsoft.

“Despite being basic $40 digital re-releases with zero new features, both titles immediately shot into the Circana U.S. Top 10 for weekly active users. They are printing money off of work completed over a decade ago.

“As a developer who actually worked on both Black Ops and Black Ops 2, seeing these charts is bittersweet. I poured my life into those games, spending countless, brutal hours in crunch alongside an incredibly talented team to make sure they were perfect.

“Seeing our blood, sweat, and tears still dominating the charts in 2026 is amazing, but its (sic) hard to watch the suits rake in giant financial windfalls from our old code while the actual creators don’t see a dime of it.”

Goslin went on to argue that the wealth should be distributed and developers who worked on the original games should get royalty payments, like in books, movies, and music. “If executives are getting massive bonuses off the longevity of these classics, that wealth needs to be shared retroactively. Legacy revenue should mean legacy rewards for the devs who survived the crunch to build them,” Goslin said.

There is no indication that Xbox will create a royalty payment system video games, but Goslin's post is well-timed, as it comes amid a surge in AI-generated ports of classic games on browsers. Indeed, Microsoft itself has appeared to take notice, announcing the Xbox Labs project in acknowledgement of the explosion in AI ports that have emerged in recent weeks.

Given the success of Black Ops 1 and 2 on PlayStation this summer, Activision will be keen to double down on similar re-releases. Chief marketing officer Tyler Bahl recently told The Game Business that the publisher had learnt a valuable lesson.

"We are definitely leaning into the nostalgia of playing with your friends,” Bahl said. “The Black Ops ports were huge successes. We thought they would do well, we didn’t think they would do that well. But you can see that pent-up demand of being able to get back to the good old days of playing with your friends on a Friday night and having fun. MW4 does that.

"We took a lot of learnings from [those ports] and are starting to apply them to not only this game, but future games."

In the shorter term, Modern Warfare 4, which closes out the rebooted Modern Warfare saga, comes out October 23. Will Activision release ports of the classic Modern Warfare games next summer, ahead of the next mainline entry in the franchise?

articles.title: Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2 Confirms a Popular Theory From the Game
articles.summary: In Netflix's Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2, a popular fan theory from Cyberpunk 2077 has been confirmed. Let’s talk about cyberpsychosis…
articles.body:
Full spoilers follow for Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2 , which is available now on Netflix.

When Cyberpunk Edgerunners premiered in 2022 , fans discovered a phenomenal season of television. Not only was it one of the best sci-fi shows of all time, but also a prime example of a video game adaptation done right, with just enough connections to the source material that they don’t impact the show’s story but still provide some nods for longtime fans. More importantly, it captured the essence of CD Projekt Red’s Cyberpunk 2077 , from its themes to its world, while also delivering an emotionally devastating story through stunning visuals — and a whole lot of brutal violence.

Edgerunners 2, which is designed as a standalone sequel series, does things a bit differently. This season still offers high levels of gore and violence, incredible animation, and themes of the evil of corporations and how they destroy everything they touch. What it does differently is incorporate into its plot not only the story of the first season of Edgerunners, but even elements from Cyberpunk 2077. That’s because a big part of Edgerunners 2 deals with Soulkiller, a program introduced in Cyberpunk 2077 as capable of digitizing the mind of a person and storing it on a chip. When inserted in another person, the digital entity from the chip slowly takes over its host and eventually kills the body’s original mind. Though it is very much a death sentence, fans of the game have long theorized that there might be an unintentional side benefit to Soulkiller — namely, a cure for cyberpsychosis.

In the world of the show and game, cyberpsychosis is a dissociative disorder that affects humans who have replaced much of their organic bodies with cybernetics. As the body rejects the chrome parts, cyberpsychosis starts to affect their minds, to the point where they no longer see themselves as people, but rather as machines with replaceable parts. This disorder manifests as an outburst where the victim disassociates and becomes violent, their brain taken over by hallucinations. In the world of Edgerunners, cyberpsychosis is portrayed as something unavoidable, a forgone conclusion the moment you start replacing your body with cybernetics. You can’t prevent it, and you can’t stop it.

But what if you can? According to a popular fan theory, the main character of Cyberpunk 2077, V, never experiences cyberpsychosis because of their interaction with the chip containing the Soulkiller program. It is the digitized entity within the chip that heals V’s emerging cyberpsychosis, as it is programmed to prepare its host body in order to take over it. Without the chip and the Soulkiller entity, V would succumb to cyberpsychosis.

We see this happen in the second half of Edgerunners 2. This season, we’re introduced to Talia, a young woman suffering from a serious if undisclosed illness. Additionally, Talia’s cybernetic implants have her on the verge of cyberpsychosis, with a doctor saying she will be lost at any minute. And yet, the moment she comes in contact with a chip containing a Soulkiller entity known as Capri, Talia’s health improves significantly and at an abnormal rate. Her brain is healed, her body is repaired, and cyberpsychosis is no longer an issue — until the chip is eventually removed and Talia reverts back to how she was, with her future uncertain.

Granted, Soulkiller is portrayed in Edgerunners as more of a weapon than anything else. Capri is described as an amalgamation of different digital constructs, which seems more like an AI made out of several individuals rather than a single one. She’s designed specifically to be the ultimate killing machine, but in addition to destroying her host body’s previous consciousness, the test subjects all die within days of getting the Capri chip inserted. This is why the Arasaka Corporation was going after people like Talia and David from Season 1, as they are known to have a high tolerance for cybernetics.

Cyberpunk Edgerunners Season 2 takes a different approach to adapting the world of Cyberpunk 2077. Though still very much an original story, this season is more intrinsically connected to the game; it feels more like a side story happening during the events of the game that the player simply didn’t get to witness. The use of the Soulkiller program serves to connect the show and the game in an interesting way without taking away from either of the separate stories. Instead, knowing the larger story of the Soulkiller from Cyberpunk 2077 makes the story of Talia and Capri hit harder because it’s one of countless similar stories in Night City.

Sure, this season doesn’t have a story as emotionally resonant as David’s from the first season, but it still very much tells an effective tale about people who get screwed by corporations. Talia may come from a family of money and power, but that can’t save her. Night City devours everyone and everything within it, and there’s no winning in that place… Though having a Soulkiller chip might help a bit if you are on the verge of cyberpsychosis.

articles.title: Stupid Never Dies Blends a Wacky Tone with Aggressive Gameplay to Create a Unique Pop-Punk Action Game
articles.body:
Stupid Never Dies is a single-player action game built on one philosophy: attack, attack, and attack some more. After playing the demo, it’s clear that all the game’s mechanics are built around rewarding aggressive play, giving gameplay a sense of momentum and progress.

You play as Davy, the world’s weakest zombie who needs to fight his way through layers of a monster-filled dungeon to take down KOM (the King of Monsters) and save a frozen girl he fell in love with at first sight. Oh, and you enter the dungeon by being flushed down a toilet. That should give you a pretty good idea of the tone, which is quirky, chaotic, and paired with a pop-punk visual style that gives the game its own unique vibe.

“How does the world’s weakest zombie manage to defeat these monsters?” you may be wondering. Well, that’s where Stupid Never Dies’ gameplay systems become the star of the show. Davy begins with a base Zombie Style that has regular and heavy attacks, a parry, and a vomit ability that can hit enemies in a row in front of you.

The parry ability (called a Stupid Parry) is important and should be used regularly, since a successful parry allows you to unleash a strong counter. You take some damage when you parry, but that lost HP is recoverable if you Bite an enemy. Landing any attack fills the Bite gauge at the bottom of the screen, and once the gauge is full, you can Bite any enemy.

Bites are powerful attacks that also replenish all your current recoverable damage and a bit of extra HP. Recoverable damage becomes actual damage over time, so you need to use Bite quickly to keep your HP topped up. This gameplay loop rewards aggressiveness, since you use parries to keep damage recoverable, land counterattacks and basic attacks to fill your gauge, and then use a Bite to get all your health back. There’s no pausing between fights to heal yourself, you need to do it in combat by staying on the offensive.

That’s not all Bites are good for, though. They can also be used to eat enemy cores to steal their abilities or combat styles. Each enemy type has a core, and eating different cores has different effects. A normal enemy will give you an Instant Skill, a one-time use ability. An elite enemy gives you access to their Style, allowing Davy to transform into it and use its unique abilities.

There will be 11 different enemy types whose Style you can steal in the game’s full release, and their gameplay varies significantly. As a Werewolf, your movement and attacks are much faster, parries can unleash a flurry of counterstrikes, and you can wall jump to get to otherwise unreachable parts of the map to find shortcuts or treasure chests. As a Harpy, you can double jump, glide through the air, fire ranged projectiles, and gain a longer-range dodge.

If it wasn’t already clear, these aren’t merely cosmetic changes or stat boosts, each Style legitimately alters how you move and fight. You can swap out your equipped Style whenever you acquire a new one, and you can transform at any time, including in the middle of a fight. So it’s wise to consistently test which Styles work best in which situations and against which enemies, and strategically switch between them to take advantage of their strengths.

Each time you dive into the dungeon, Davy will reset back to Level 1 and just have access to his base Zombie form. But each run also boosts how quickly you level up in a system that developer GPTRACK50 Inc. refers to as “blazing fast growth.” The boost depends on how far you got and how many enemies you defeated in your previous run.

True to its name, the difference in leveling speed is significant and noticeable. After only a handful of runs in the demo, my EXP boost was over 400% and I was gaining levels after every fight. When I first made it to the boss Afreet, I was level 10 (and he kicked my ass). During my last run before writing this article, I devoured him and finished the fight at level 21.

The sped up leveling helps the sense of momentum encouraged by the aggressive gameplay, since you’re always pushing forward, even after a failed run. Each run builds on the ones that came before it, and the boosts are cumulative, so no run is wasted.

Rapid leveling is also important because each run through the dungeon has a countdown timer. If you run out of time, you’ll die, get sent back to your base, and lose the items you gained during that run. There are Landing Areas at certain spots in the dungeon, and if you reach one, you can escape while keeping your items. So you have to weigh the risk vs. reward of pushing farther into the dungeon or getting out while you can.

If you successfully get out of the dungeon with the items you gathered, you can use them to create OT Gear for body hacks, a system where you can replace Davy’s body parts with technology that gives him new abilities. In my time with the demo, I saw abilities that included a deployable barrier, a spinning attack that lunges you forward, and saws that rotate in a circle around you.

You can also use ingredients you gather to create new Zombie Skills, which are stat boosts and other boons that you can activate during a run. When you reach certain levels, you’ll be given the option to activate one of three Zombie Skills that are randomly selected from the ones you’ve unlocked.

Eating bosses for the first time awards you with special materials that you can turn in to unlock unique upgrades. Defeating Afreet allowed me to unlock a Zombie Skill that gave my attacks enhanced knockback and gave them extra damage if I used them to knock enemies into walls.

Between all the different Styles, body hacks, and Zombie Skills, there are a ton of different customization options to try and see what fits your playstyle best. And all of these systems are sure to be expanded in the final release compared to what’s available in the demo version.

If you want to give Stupid Never Dies a try for yourself, an updated free demo is available now on Steam and PlayStation 5 . The full game releases on October 21 on those same two platforms.

articles.title: We Build LEGO PlayStation, a Near 1:1 Scale Replica of Sony's Classic Console
articles.summary: We build the LEGO PlayStation set, a near 1:1 scale replica of Sony's entry into the world of video games.
articles.body:
I love LEGO sets based on retro game consoles. They combine two of my favorite things: video games (for obvious reasons) and LEGO sets, with impossibly clever construction mechanics and plenty of Easter eggs.

The latest retro system to become a buildable set is LEGO PlayStation, a near 1:1 scale model of Sony’s original hardware. Now, it may seem like a foregone conclusion today, but the success of the PlayStation was no sure thing when it launched in 1994 in Japan and in 1995 in the US. Many electronics companies had dabbled in the world of video games and failed quickly, with nothing to show for it.

But young me? I was a believer in PlayStation from the start. I remember buying the little gray machine at launch and pouring hundreds of hours into games like Jumping Flash, Battle Arena Toshinden, Street Fighter: The Movie (the game), Twisted Metal, Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, Doom, Resident Evil 2, Oddworld: Abe’s Odyssey, Medal of Honor, Metal Gear Solid, Final Fantasy VII through IX (remember when three mainline Final Fantasies could come out in a single generation?) and on and on. Man, what an incredible library.

The PS1 provided all the gaming I needed through the latter half of the '90s. I didn’t buy another console until the PlayStation 2 came out after the turn of the millennium.

LEGO PlayStation comes with 1,911 bricks divided into 14 paper bags and takes around six hours to build. Despite the mostly gray exterior, it’s a fun, surprisingly colorful construction from start to finish. It uses a number of clever building techniques along the way, and includes a few delightful Easter eggs.

Even the box for this set is an Easter egg of sorts. It calls back to the box of the original PlayStation.

The process of the build is about what you'd expect: you start by completing the base of the console, and then build your way to the top. But inside of the machine, you first lay down the red, yellow, and blue PS logo, and then build and insert all sorts of colorful little chips and electronic components — many of which you immediately cover up. Unlike the real console, however, you can see some of these "electronics" when you lift the lid.

Also hidden inside the console are two dioramas that slide out on smooth tracks. These are like secret drawers that feature colorful micro-scale worlds for Ape Escape and Gran Turismo, two popular games from the platform. While I didn’t play either of those games back in the day and would have preferred nods to, say, Resident Evil and Metal Gear Solid, they’re still a fun inclusion and I’m sure many fans will appreciate them more than I do.

The set includes one small sheet of stickers. I’ve complained about stickers in LEGO sets before (particularly in LEGO Jurassic Park Jeep Wrangler and LEGO Winnie the Pooh ), but they’re more of a minor irritant here. All of the stickers go on the dioramas, which are hidden by default.

All of the most important and visible images on this set — the PlayStation and Sony logos, and the controller’s face button shapes — are pre-printed on the pieces. This is a huge relief for me personally, as I can’t line up a sticker on a LEGO piece perfectly to save my life.

The finished product looks remarkably like a 1:1 representation of the original hardware. If you view it from a distance, you’d be forgiven for thinking it was an actual PS1. I dug up my original PlayStation to compare the two devices (I could only find my DualShock controller, not the original). The LEGO set looks incredibly similar to the real thing from almost every angle. The main difference is the LEGO set lacks the RCA ports in the back, which isn’t a big deal (see the slideshow below for more comparison pics).

Even the Power and Open buttons on the finished set “work.” Pressing Power lifts a little green translucent rod into view, right where the green power light is on the original hardware. Pressing the Open button releases a latch that, thanks to a spring-loaded mechanism, raises the disc lid, just like it does on the original.

I have a few minor complaints about LEGO PlayStation. My Open button sticks when I press it all the way in, so the lid won’t close unless I fiddle with the button to make it pop back out. The controller also looks a little janky, but I understand it’s hard or impossible to make an exact replica LEGO version of something so curvy.

If you’re a gamer of a certain age and have fond memories of playing then-newfangled CD-based games on an original PlayStation, I can wholeheartedly recommend this set. It would also make a fine gift, if someone you know falls into that category.

LEGO PlayStation is available for $179.99 at the LEGO Store and PlayStation Direct .

Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's LEGO coverage and maintains the upcoming release dates articles for video games , LEGO sets , and 4K Blu-rays . You can follow him on Bluesky .
